title: The realization–singular unit is a realization weak equivalence
statement: Use simplicial sets, geometric realization, and weak homotopy equivalences as in [def-cbc-enhanced-diagrams-cones], in a fixed universe large enough for the sets of continuous maps below. For a topological space $T$, define the singular simplicial set by $\operatorname{Sing}(T)_n=\operatorname{Cont}(|\Delta^n|,T)$, with operators given by precomposition with the affine maps of topological simplices. For every small simplicial set $X$, let $u_X:X\to\operatorname{Sing}(|X|)$ be the simplicial map taking $x\in X_n$ to the continuous characteristic map $t\mapsto[x,t]$ into the quotient realization. Then $|u_X|:|X|\to|\operatorname{Sing}(|X|)|$ induces a bijection on path components and isomorphisms on all based homotopy groups at every basepoint of $|X|$. No Kan, finiteness, connectedness or nonemptiness assumption on $X$ is imposed.

source.place: Theorem 3.6.4.1 (Milnor), Kerodon Tag 0142; Corollary 3.6.4.3, Kerodon Tag 03X7, identifies the geometric-realization convention for weak equivalences. Read online 2026-10-17; not archived in literature/. No Stacks tag for this theorem; these are Kerodon tags.

proof.text: Put $T=|X|$ and $A=\operatorname{Sing}(T)$. Define $\epsilon:|A|\to T$ by $\epsilon([\sigma,t])=\sigma(t)$. Precomposition gives $\epsilon([\sigma\alpha_*,t])=\sigma(\alpha_*t)$, so this is well-defined on the realization relation and continuous by its quotient topology. The same relation gives $(u_Xx)\alpha_*=u_X(X(\alpha)x)$, so the characteristic maps form a simplicial map. On every representative, $\epsilon(|u_X|([x,t]))=\epsilon([u_Xx,t])=[x,t]$; hence $\epsilon\circ|u_X|=\mathrm{id}_T$. It remains to compute the maps induced by this particular $\epsilon$.

source.place: Theorem 3.6.7, proof, printed p. 99: evaluation map; explicit quotient and triangle-identity calculation supplied here. The item itself is Kerodon Tag 0142.

proof.text: The simplicial set $A$ is Kan. Indeed, the realization/singular adjunction of [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits] sends a horn map $\Lambda_i^m\to A$ to a continuous map $|\Lambda_i^m|\to T$. For $m\geq1$ its realized pair is $(D^{m-1}\times[0,1],D^{m-1}\times\{0\})$. Projection to the bottom face, conjugated by this homeomorphism of pairs, is a continuous retraction $r:|\Delta^m|\to|\Lambda_i^m|$. Composing the adjoint horn map with $r$ and transposing back gives a filler, since $r$ restricts to the identity. The adjunction applies because $T$ is a k-space by the same node. This handles all inner and outer horns, including $m=1$, without requiring $T$ to be nonempty.

source.place: Section 3.1 adjunction; realized horn pair before Proposition 3.2.3; Theorem 3.6.7 uses fibrancy of Sing. The retraction argument is written out.

proof.text: Fix $t_0\in T$ and $n\geq1$. Write $Q_n=\Delta^n/\partial\Delta^n$, pointed at the collapsed boundary. By the adjunction and preservation of colimits in [lem-coef-realization-finite-limits], a pointed map $Q_n\to A$ is exactly a continuous $a:|\Delta^n|\to T$ constant at $t_0$ on $|\partial\Delta^n|$. The realized simplex pair is $(D^n,S^{n-1})$. Use the same pair identification as in the realization comparison [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre]; equivalently change from ball to cube by the radial homeomorphism along rays from their centers. Thus these $a$, modulo homotopies constant on the boundary, give the underlying set of $\pi_n(T,t_0)$ in the cubical convention. This identifies representatives, rather than asserting a comparison of homotopy groups without checking homotopies.

source.place: Example 3.2.2.7 (Tag 00VR), with the simplex-pair and representative conventions of Hovey Proposition 3.6.3.

proof.text: The correspondence in step 3 identifies exactly the two homotopy relations. A pointed simplicial homotopy $h:Q_n\times\Delta^1\to A$ is adjoint to a continuous map $|Q_n\times\Delta^1|\to T$; the homeomorphism of [lem-coef-simplicial-realization-cylinder] turns this into $|Q_n|\times[0,1]\to T$, constant at $t_0$ on the basepoint cylinder. Conversely, given a boundary-fixed continuous homotopy $H:|\Delta^n|\times[0,1]\to T$, assign to a $k$-simplex $(\alpha:[k]\to[n],\theta:[k]\to[1])$ the singular simplex $z\mapsto H(\alpha_*z,\sum_{\theta(j)=1}z_j)$. If $\alpha$ lies in the boundary this is constant at $t_0$, so the formula descends to $Q_n\times\Delta^1$; coordinate sums under precomposition prove the simplicial identities. At the two ends it gives the two original representatives. Hence it descends both ways to a bijection $\Phi_n:\pi_n^s(A,t_0)\to\pi_n(T,t_0)$ of underlying sets, also when simplicial homotopy is defined as its generated equivalence relation.

source.place: Example 3.2.2.7 (Tag 00VR); explicit expansion of the homotopy assertion in Hovey Theorem 3.6.7, printed p. 99.

proof.text: Apply [lem-coef-kan-realization-serre] to the Kan complex $A$ of step 2. Its stated comparison is an isomorphism $\rho_n:\pi_n^s(A,t_0)\to\pi_n(|A|,t_0)$ induced by realizing representatives. Evaluation on a representative gives $\epsilon([a,z])=a(z)$, so $\epsilon_{*,t_0}\rho_n=\Phi_n$. The preceding bijection and the bijectivity of $\rho_n$ imply that $\epsilon_{*,t_0}$ is bijective. Postcomposition commutes with concatenation of cubes, so it is a group homomorphism and therefore a group isomorphism. This avoids any choice between opposite conventions for multiplication on simplicial fundamental groups. For components, the same cited node identifies $\pi_0(|A|)$ with vertices modulo edges. Vertices of $A$ are exactly points of $T$ and its edges are exactly continuous paths in $T$ (parametrize $|\Delta^1|$ by its second coordinate). Thus evaluation induces a bijection $\pi_0(|A|)\to\pi_0(T)$.

source.place: Proposition 3.6.3 and Theorem 3.6.7, printed pp. 97–99; the latter computes evaluation on homotopy groups using the adjunction. Component and group-law checks expanded here.

proof.text: Here are explicit maps needed to extend the calculation from singular vertices to an arbitrary point $y\in|A|$. Represent $y=[\sigma,z]$ and choose a vertex $e_0$ of that simplex. Set $v=[\sigma,e_0]$ and $\gamma(s)=[\sigma,(1-s)e_0+sz]$, a continuous path from $v$ to $y$. Form the quotient spaces $E=(|A|\amalg[0,1])/(1\sim y)$ and $F=(T\amalg[0,1])/(1\sim\epsilon(y))$, pointed at the new endpoint $0$. Define $r_E:E\to|A|$ to be the identity on $|A|$ and constant $y$ on the interval, and $h_E:E\to|A|$ to be the identity on $|A|$ and $\gamma$ on the interval. Define $r_F,h_F$ using $\epsilon(y)$ and $\epsilon\gamma$. These maps are continuous by the quotient universal property, since the two coproduct branches agree at the attachment. Let $i_E:|A|\hookrightarrow E$ be inclusion. A homotopy from $1_E$ to $i_Er_E$ fixes $|A|$ and sends an interval point $s$ at parameter $a$ to $s+a(1-s)$ in the attached interval. A homotopy from $1_E$ to $i_Eh_E$ fixes $|A|$ and sends $s$ to $s+2a(1-s)$ for $0\leq a\leq\tfrac12$, while for $\tfrac12\leq a\leq1$ it sends $s$ to $\gamma(1-(2a-1)(1-s))$ in the original summand. The two formulas agree at $a=\tfrac12$ (both are the attachment point $y$) and at $s=1$; their endpoints are respectively $1_E$ and $i_Eh_E$. The same formulas, with $\epsilon\gamma$ and $\epsilon(y)$, give homotopies for $r_F$ and $h_F$. Joint continuity on each quotient follows by transposing in the compact, locally compact parameter interval with [lem-coef-compact-open-currying], descending the continuous transposes, and evaluating again. Thus all four maps are homotopy equivalences, with no stationary-basepoint assumption.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed pp. 341–342, basepoint transport. The attached-interval construction and both homotopies are an explicit agent expansion; currying justifies product topology on quotient homotopies.

proof.text: Define $\epsilon^+:E\to F$ by $\epsilon$ on the original space and the identity on the attached interval. The quotient formulas give strictly $r_F\epsilon^+=\epsilon r_E$ and $h_F\epsilon^+=\epsilon h_E$, with all maps pointed at the indicated images of the new endpoint. By [lem-coef-homotopy-equivalence-weak] the four maps $r_E,r_F,h_E,h_F$ induce group isomorphisms in every positive degree at that endpoint. Step 5 already makes $\epsilon_{*,v}$ an isomorphism. The second equality therefore makes $(\epsilon^+)_{*,0}$ an isomorphism, and the first equality then makes $\epsilon_{*,y}$ an isomorphism. These deductions are cancellation in two commutative squares of group homomorphisms, so no uncited change-of-basepoint theorem is being invoked. Together with step 5, evaluation is bijective on components and isomorphic on all homotopy groups at every point of $|A|$.

source.place: Section 4.1, printed p. 342, homotopy equivalences and nonstationary basepoints; explicit attached-interval cancellation applies the statement of lem-coef-homotopy-equivalence-weak.

proof.text: For every $x\in|X|$, the identity of step 1 induces $\epsilon_{*,|u_X|(x)}\circ(|u_X|)_{*,x}=\mathrm{id}_{\pi_n(|X|,x)}$. The first factor is an isomorphism by step 7, so $(|u_X|)_{*,x}$ is its inverse. On path components the identical equation and the bijection of step 5 show that $|u_X|$ induces the inverse bijection. This proves all clauses of the statement. If $X$ is empty, then $|X|$, its singular set and its iterated realization are empty, the component functions are the unique bijections, and no based assertion is required. No step imposed Kan, finiteness or connectedness on $X$.
